280: I can tell you anything about two hundred years ago. Today, I'm completely lost.
281: I file the past into tiny boxes. The present keeps refusing to fit in one.
282: I'm an expert on a century I never lived in and a stranger to this one.
283: Ask me about the year 1820. Ask me about this morning and I go quite still.
284: I wear soft gloves to handle things older than most nations. Then I go home and drop a plate.
285: I read handwriting from long before you were born. My own notes defeat me by lunchtime.
286: I've spent decades organizing the past. It's the only era I feel at home in.
287: I can date a letter to the exact decade. I could not tell you today's date.
288: The past is neatly labeled and boxed. The present is out there, unsorted, loud.
289: I keep two hundred years in careful order and my own week in total chaos.
290: People come to me for history. Nobody comes to me for the news, and rightly so.
291: I keep the room colder than anyone likes, so the paper can outlive us all in comfort.
292: Three people visited the archive this year. Each of them I now consider a close friend.
293: My expertise stops precisely at the moment I was born, and it has learned nothing since.
294: I know what happened in a distant year better than what happened at breakfast.
295: Everything here smells faintly of two centuries ago. I stopped noticing. Guests never do.
296: I preserve the old world beautifully. The new one keeps arriving without labels.
297: I can find a letter from long ago in seconds. My keys, however, are gone forever.
298: No food, no drink, no sudden movements near the documents. The past bruises very easily.
299: Some pages would crumble at a sneeze. So I have learned, professionally, never to sneeze.
300: I fly to places all day. I have never once been asked to stay and look around.
301: The passengers all know where they're going. I just point the plane and hope they agree.
302: I have landed in more cities than I can name. I saw the runway of each one, briefly.
303: People thank me for a smooth flight. I nod, as if smoothness was my decision and not luck.
304: I've flown over every mountain worth flying over. From up here they all look like wrinkles.
305: My whole job is to leave. I have gotten very good at leaving. Staying, less so.
306: I announce the weather like I checked it myself. I did not. A screen told me.
307: I've seen a thousand sunrises from the sky. I would trade some for one full night of sleep.
308: Everyone claps when we land. I appreciate it. Landing is, in fairness, the important part.
309: I know the sky better than my own street. My own street keeps moving the parking.
310: I fly for a living, and yet I still get nervous when someone else drives to the airport.
311: The best part of the job is the view. The second best is that no one can hand me their bags.
312: I have flown for years. I still cannot tell you what the little dial on the left actually does.
313: I take people to their reunions, meetings, and beaches. I go back to the airport.
314: My office has the finest view in the world, and no place at all to hang a picture.
315: I've circled the same tower forty times waiting to land. We became close, that tower and I.
316: I carry hundreds of people and remember none. They carry snacks and remember everything.
317: People ask if I ever get bored up there. Only when nothing is trying to go wrong.
318: I spend my days above the clouds. It is lovely, and it is also just a very high desk.
319: I have a hat, a schedule, and absolutely no idea what my passengers packed.
